idiom_name: ownership: the state lives in the struct that owns it and is dropped with that owner; wider sharing is an explicit Rc<RefCell<T>> / Arc<Mutex<T>> opt-in
implementation_notes: Rust's ownership system already implements the pattern's core: every value has exactly one owner, that owner lives in a scope, references cannot outlive the data they point at, and the value is dropped when the owner goes out of scope - so the smallest-scope placement is enforced by the compiler rather than chosen. The classic structure (a shared mutable state hub) can only be built by asking for it explicitly: Rc<RefCell<T>> for single-threaded shared mutability, Arc<Mutex<T>> across threads; both are visible in the type. In an application the state therefore lives in the struct that owns the widget, screen or session, with per-widget state as fields of the widget struct and per-request values as locals. Reserve interior mutability for the places where sharing is genuine (observer lists, framework handles), not as a default way to make code compile.
pitfalls: RefCell moves borrow checking to run time: a second overlapping mutable borrow compiles but panics, so interior mutability converts a compile-time guarantee into a runtime failure mode.
Rc/Arc cycles are never dropped (the classic shared observer graph leaks); back-references need Weak, and Arc<Mutex<T>> introduces lock hazards (deadlock, poisoning) that plain ownership avoids.
Mutable globals exist (static mut, OnceLock/LazyLock or framework equivalents) but require unsafe or locking and are exactly the over-lifted state the pattern warns against.
